doc.title: Hal Galper interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 27, 2022

title: How musical growth occurs: neurons, Brecker, and a student's Spain trip
summary: His theory is that attraction to a player lights preset neurons; he tells how a student copied Michael Brecker's solo and returned a changed player.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Did you have any epiphanies along the way with this question?

Countless. That’s what led me to forward motion but it took me a long time to realize that was what I was interested in. I’ve been working on a new book which I’m probably never going to finish, of essays. And one of the essays is on — oh shit what was I talking about? Sorry.
Epiphanies and mind and ear, and the first beat.

Oh all right. So I am working on one of these articles. I have a theory about how musical decisions are made. Generally most decisions are made below the level of consciousness anyway. Right? So [damn it Hal, get back] where was I? You’re going to have to —
Well we were talking about the first beat, and you were talking about how most decisions seem to be made in the subconscious perhaps?

Yeah. But I have a theory about how musical growth occurs. That’s what it was. Because when you listen to somebody the assumption has been that you’re trying to learn something from that musician. If you’re attracted to a musician that’s because I feel like you have to learn there’s something about that musician that is attracting you to him. So I have a belief that you’re born with neutral — a whole bunch of neutral neurological neurons waiting to be stimulated from the environment. It’s a thing of like the environment stimulates the growth of these neurons. When I heard that George Shearing record that lit up those neurons. They were waiting there to get lit up. All right? Let me give you a case in point. I had a band with an alto player and he played beautifully, a beautiful young, one of my top ex-students. But for years I’ve been trying to get him to emote more, to articulate larger than life, to, you know, get his metal buzzing and all that stuff. I was constantly on his case and he just never got it together. So the band was over a couple of years and we still communicate all the time with my ex-students. And he said, “Oh Hal, I’m going to Spain, I’ve got this contest in Spain that I’m going to go to, and you have to pick somebody’s solo to memorize and play it.” So he picked Mike Brecker’s solo on my recording of “Triple Play” with my quintet. He picked Michael Brecker. All

right? He went to the festival, he came back, he said, “Well I didn’t win.” I said, “Well play something for me.” You know. When he played he had everything I had been trying to get out of him for years. So how did that happen? Why did he pick Michael Brecker? Because Michael Brecker set off a particular neural neuron, right, that led him to pick Michael Brecker. Because that’s what he needed at that moment was to copy Michael Brecker and learn how to play with that level of intensity. Because he came back from Spain a different horn player. It’s out of our hands. You’re not trying to learn something from the artist you’re copying, the artist is trying to teach you something about yourself which is how you hear. And you have a resonance with these neurons, they’re just waiting for the environment — it’s a combination of preset and environment you know. That’s nothing new you know. It’s not a new concept.

My neurons are spinning, Hal. But it leads me to a guy that made literally — did that for me, and it was Cannonball Adderley. And I remember, I guess I was 15 or 16 but that’s what happened to me. I never put that description to it but that’s exactly what it was.
